reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A cortical pseudobulbar palsy caused by bilateral damage to the anterior opercular (frontal operculum) regions
Produces loss of voluntary control of the face, tongue, pharynx, and masticatory muscles, with anarthria, drooling, and dysphagia
The defining feature is automatic-voluntary dissociation: patients cannot move these muscles on command yet retain automatic and emotional movements such as spontaneous laughing, crying, or yawning
Volitional speech is severely impaired or absent despite comprehension being preserved
Most commonly results from bilateral strokes affecting the opercular cortex, but is also caused by infection, trauma, tumour, and rarely a reversible epileptic form in children
Distinguished from brainstem (true) bulbar palsy by the preserved automatic movements and cortical localisation
Management is supportive, focused on the underlying cause, secure nutrition and airway, and speech and swallow rehabilitation
reference.pathophysiology: Foix-Chavany-Marie syndrome arises from bilateral lesions of the anterior operculum, the cortical region overlying the insula that controls voluntary movement of the lower face, tongue, jaw, pharynx, and larynx. Because voluntary corticobulbar control of these muscles is disrupted while the separate pathways mediating automatic and emotionally driven movements (involving limbic and extrapyramidal circuits) remain intact, patients show the striking automatic-voluntary dissociation. The commonest cause is sequential or simultaneous bilateral ischaemic stroke of the opercular cortex, though inflammatory, traumatic, neoplastic, and, in children, epileptic and reversible aetiologies are recognised. Preserved comprehension reflects sparing of language cortex outside the affected motor opercular regions.
additionalDifferentials: Pseudobulbar palsy from other bilateral corticobulbar lesions
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with bulbar involvement
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain demonstrating bilateral opercular lesions
CT or MR angiography to assess cerebrovascular disease in stroke-related cases
Electroencephalography, especially in children, to identify the epileptic (reversible) form
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis where an infective or inflammatory cause is suspected
Swallow assessment (e.g. videofluoroscopy) to guide feeding safety
redFlags: Aspiration and airway compromise from severe dysphagia
Acute onset indicating a new stroke requiring urgent assessment
Rapid progression suggesting an expanding lesion or encephalitis
Complete inability to manage oral secretions
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the cause and extent of injury; the epileptic childhood form may be reversible, whereas established bilateral opercular strokes often leave persistent anarthria and dysphagia requiring long-term rehabilitation and nutritional support.
pitfalls: Mistaking the syndrome for a brainstem bulbar palsy and missing the cortical localisation
Misinterpreting preserved automatic smiling or crying as intact voluntary function
Overlooking aspiration risk because comprehension is preserved
Failing to consider the reversible epileptic form in children
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Treat the underlying cause — hyperacute stroke reperfusion with thrombolysis or thrombectomy where eligible for the common bilateral opercular infarcts, and antiseizure medication for the reversible childhood epileptic form
Establish secondary stroke prevention with antiplatelet (or anticoagulant where cardioembolic) therapy, a statin and vascular risk-factor control to prevent a completing contralateral event

Protect the airway and nutrition with formal swallow assessment, texture modification and enteral feeding via nasogastric tube then gastrostomy when dysphagia is unsafe, to prevent aspiration pneumonia
Support communication through speech and language therapy and augmentative and alternative communication, given anarthria despite preserved comprehension
Manage drooling with antimuscarinic therapy and positioning, alongside regular oral care
Coordinate multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and dietetics
Escalate urgently for airway compromise, respiratory failure or recurrent aspiration
